title: Why So Many Kids Are Checking Out of School
author: Katie Martin
summary: Katie Martin argues that the chronic absenteeism gripping American schools is not a compliance problem but a design problem — a signal that the traditional school model has decoupled from students' lives, identities, and futures. Drawing on personal experience, educator testimony, and the research framework from The Disengaged Teen, she identifies four student archetypes — Resisters, Passengers, Achievers, and Explorers — and argues that schools are inadvertently producing the first three. The article traces how the erosion of meaningful school experiences (field days, traditions, community rituals), combined with the rise of AI that can complete assignments and enable high grades without engagement, has rendered the case for attendance increasingly fragile. Martin distinguishes between disengagement from learning and disengagement from the system, insisting young people are not lazy but are responding rationally to systems that feel irrelevant and disconnected. She calls on educators and school designers to stop layering more compliance onto a broken model and instead rebuild schools into environments worthy of student presence.
points: The attendance crisis is a design failure, not a motivation failure: students are disengaging from systems that no longer feel connected to their lives, not from learning itself.
AI has sharpened an existing contradiction — students can now earn top grades without attending class, exposing that seat time and compliance were never reliable proxies for learning.

Martin's four-archetype framework (Resister, Passenger, Achiever, Explorer) reframes 'lazy teenagers' as rational actors adapting to misaligned environments, with Explorers as the target state schools should be designed to cultivate.

The disappearance of communal rituals (assemblies, field days, performances) under pressure to maximize instructional minutes has stripped schools of the social-emotional glue that once made attendance feel worthwhile.

Tightening rules and surveillance is the wrong lever: harsher attendance policies treat a symptom while leaving the root design problem untouched, and Martin explicitly warns this approach risks missing the deeper message students are sending.
quotes: Young people are not disengaging from learning. In many cases, they are disengaging from systems that no longer feel connected to their lives, identities, relationships, or futures.

If AI can complete assignments, what is the value of the work students are being asked to do? If students are physically sitting in school but mentally disengaged, what is the value of the time they are spending there?

Today, many students experience school as a series of disconnected assignments, compliance tasks, and performance measures. Meanwhile, educators are trying to hold together a system under enormous strain.

Students tell me their teachers are using AI to create assignments and grade work. Teachers tell me students are using AI to complete those assignments. Families still want their children to succeed, but the traditional formula — work hard, get good grades, get a stable job — no longer feels guaranteed.

The goal is not simply to force compliance or improve attendance numbers. The goal ought to be to create learning environments that help more young people become Explorers: engaged, curious, connected, and motivated to learn because they see meaning in what they are doing.

The attendance crisis is not just a policy problem. It is a design problem. And if we continue responding only with tighter rules, harsher consequences, more surveillance, and stronger compliance measures, we risk missing the deeper message students are sending us.

One of the most important shifts we need to make is reframing how we think about disengaged teenagers. Too often, we label students as lazy, unmotivated, or apathetic when, in reality, disengagement is often a response to the system itself.
